title: Trump Wants to Spend $700 Million to Bring Back Coal Power — But Is That a Good Idea?
summary:
Did you know that coal used to provide more than half of America’s electricity? Today, it’s down to just 15%. But President Trump wants to change that — in a big way.

He’s expected to announce a nearly $700 million plan to support coal-fired power plants and coal exports. The money would help 13 existing coal plants across the country, build new ones in Alaska and West Virginia (the first new U.S. coal plants since 2013!), and even restart a plant in Maryland. It would also help finish a coal export terminal in Oakland, California.

The White House says this will support or create more than 14,000 jobs in coal, construction, rail, and shipping. Trump will use a law from the 1950s called the Defense Production Act, which lets the president take action to protect national security.

But not everyone is cheering. Environmental groups say propping up coal with taxpayer money is a bad idea. Coal is a polluting energy source — burning it releases gases that warm the planet and particles that can make people sick. Critics say this plan will lead to higher electricity bills and dirtier air.

“What’s next, a taxpayer bailout to build new phone booths?” joked one environmental leader.

Coal has been shrinking for years because natural gas is cheaper and cleaner, and renewable energy like wind and solar is growing fast. Under Trump, the government has even forced some old coal and gas plants to keep running past their retirement dates to meet rising electricity demand from data centers, AI, and electric cars.

Trump’s team says these emergency orders helped prevent blackouts during a brutal cold snap earlier this year. But environmentalists say the best thing for our air, climate, and wallets is to let old coal plants retire peacefully.

So what do you think — is bringing back coal a smart move, or should we look to the future instead?
why_it_matters: The decision to pour money into old coal power or new clean energy affects the air everyone breathes, the jobs of the future, and what climate you will live in as an adult.

background_read: For much of the 1900s, coal was America’s main fuel for electricity, but by the 2020s, cheaper natural gas and cleaner solar and wind power took its place.

President Donald Trump (who returned to office in 2025) wants to use the Defense Production Act, an old law meant for military supplies, to spend nearly $700 million on coal projects — saying it will create jobs and stop blackouts.
Environmental groups point out that burning coal worsens climate change and air pollution, and many energy experts believe the long-term future is in renewable energy, not coal.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump’s administration, coal companies, and environmental organizations.
WHAT: A plan to spend nearly $700 million to support old coal-fired plants, build new ones, and restart a closed plant, using a national security law.
WHERE: New plants would be built in Alaska and West Virginia, a coal terminal in Oakland, California, and 13 existing plants across the country.
WHY: To create about 14,000 jobs and prevent blackouts; opponents say it will raise pollution, hurt health, and cost taxpayers more.

perspectives.description: The plan could save coal mining jobs and help make sure the U.S. has enough electricity during freezing winters or heat waves.
Environmental groups warn that burning more coal will worsen climate change and air pollution, leading to higher hospital visits and electricity bills.
Energy experts note that coal has been declining for years because cleaner, cheaper options exist; spending billions to prop it up may only delay its retirement rather than reverse the trend.
